claims.text: A defect-aware model will predict electrical conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than perfect-crystal analytical approaches in the 0–200 K regime.
A defect-aware model will predict electrical conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than perfect-crystal analytical approaches in the 300–1200 K regime.
Bulk HfNbTaTiZr can be produced by spark plasma sintering of gas-atomized powder.
A low-oxygen HfNbTaTiZr state containing approximately 0.12 wt.% oxygen exists.
An intentionally oxygen-doped HfNbTaTiZr state containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen exists.
The proposed model can explicitly account for oxygen-related defects in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed model can explicitly account for dislocation density in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen in HfNbTaTiZr produces lattice distortions and defect sites such as vacancies and dislocation cores.
Oxygen-induced defects modify the electronic band structure and electron-scattering mechanisms of HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen incorporation creates defect energy levels and lattice strain that alter electron scattering and activation energies.
At low temperature, oxygen-related defects hinder conduction in HfNbTaTiZr through an ionization-limited regime.
At high temperature, oxygen-related defects act as springboards for thermal excitation of electrons across an effectively reduced gap.
The proposed high-temperature defect mechanism produces intrinsic-conduction behavior that better follows experimental trends.
The defect-aware model will predict lower cryogenic conductivities than conventional perfect-crystal models.
The conductivity behavior will exhibit a distinct transition in activation energy around room temperature.
The defect-aware model will reduce errors in both activation energies and conductivity magnitudes relative to conventional analytical models.
Perfect-crystal analytical predictions typically overestimate the conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Perfect-crystal analytical predictions fail to capture transitions between conduction mechanisms in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The expected accuracy advantage is limited to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The expected accuracy advantage applies only to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing no more than approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
